rationale: The clinicopathological analysis compares measured smell identification with autopsy-supported Lewy body and Alzheimer diagnoses. Visual hallucinations enter the diagnostic predictor comparison. It does not measure change in visual episodes after dried fig intake.

Postmortem elemental imaging localizes mercury in the visual and auditory thalamic relay nuclei. A proposed future diet diary, including fish, is separate from the actual measurements. No fig consumption or timed visual hallucination outcome was collected.

The EEG study includes 41 patients with Lewy body dementia, 21 with Alzheimer dementia and 40 controls. Alpha reactivity and cholinergic integrity are the measured contrasts. Clinical hallucination reports characterize participants without an assigned or recorded fig exposure.

The neuropathology review compares olfactory changes in Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. Its discussion of visual hallucinations refers to cited clinical and tissue associations. The paper supplies no dried fig intervention or hallucination episode measurement.

Resting network connectivity was compared against measures of impulsive behavior in a Parkinson clinic sample. Few participants had visual hallucinations, and the relevant symptom scores did not distinguish the analyzed groups. The exposure comparison was clinical impulsivity without dried fig intake.

Telephone interviews of 20 people with dementia with Lewy bodies and 25 caregivers elicited research priorities. The reported experiences and priorities do not estimate a response to dried fig or establish visual episode timing after meals.

The study relates cortical thickness to Alzheimer co-pathology in Lewy body disorders. Well-formed visual hallucinations contribute to the clinical characterization. Anatomical measures in these groups leave a dietary episode-rate effect untested.

The psychophysical experiment adjusts the contrast of visual stimuli in Parkinson participants with and without hallucinations. Discrimination under the task improves with higher contrast. The outcome is object identification, and it supplies no change in clinical hallucination frequency or fig exposure.

The retrospective 372-case autopsy cohort compares hallucination and delusion characteristics across confirmed neuropathologies. Presence, content and distress are distinct charted features. The cohort does not relate an identified food exposure to episodes.

The study combines tract tracing from patient imaging and physiological signals to characterize the nucleus basalis and cortical connectivity in Lewy body disease groups. Visual hallucinations are a diagnostic or clinical feature. The measurements concern pathways without a dried fig comparison.

Eye-tracking contrasts fixation duration and pupil size in 50 Parkinson participants and 43 controls. Visual hallucinations appear in the clinical background. The recorded fixation and pupil responses are different endpoints.

The systematic review and small case series describe Parkinson delusional jealousy with medication histories and other symptoms, including visual hallucinations in some records. The primary phenomenon is a delusion, and neither source arm examines dried fig intake.

The systematic review evaluates common SNCA variants and clinical heterogeneity. A cited retrospective comparison associates a variant with the risk of developing visual hallucinations. It gives no dietary exposure or episode contrast.

The study compares transcription profiles of human anterior cingulate tissue across Lewy body conditions. Visual symptoms partly characterize the groups. The molecular analyses do not measure a fig exposure or recurrent visual episode rate.

The autopsy study compares clinical and cognitive profiles of LATE neuropathologic change and FTLD-TDP. Visual hallucinations are retrospective symptoms distinguished by pathology. It does not follow a Parkinson culinary intervention.

The individual case describes a rare frontotemporal and progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype with a progranulin variant. The discussion places visual hallucinations within a wider diagnostic differential. There is no dried fig comparison or Parkinson episode follow-up.

Records from 331 Parkinson patients are grouped by no pain, nonfluctuating pain and fluctuating pain. The fluctuating-pain group had more people with a visual hallucination history than the no-pain group. This is symptom co-occurrence, without a fig exposure or a change in visual episodes.

The synucleinopathy review describes neuropathological diagnoses and molecular evidence. Visual hallucinations inform clinical subtyping and are discussed in relation to earlier findings. No underlying fig intervention or dietary episode contrast is reported.

The small postmortem comparison evaluates pathological proteins in Parkinson dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and control brains. Visual hallucinations distinguish descriptions of the disorders. The measured tissue markers supply no food effect.

The original postmortem comparison maps inorganic mercury and regional pathology in selected brains. Clinical visual hallucinations are discussed as a possible sign of visual pathway involvement. Tissue localization cannot identify dried fig intake or its symptom effect.

The structural imaging synthesis assesses Parkinson visual hallucination groups and compares patterns with independent receptor maps. Regional associations and receptor-map alignment do not provide an intervention, named food exposure or visual episode-rate comparison.

The study combines symptom interviews and network imaging in 35 analyzable people with Lewy body disease. It codes hallucination content, duration and frequency separately. Imaging correlations are linked to characteristics of reported phenomena, without a dietary exposure.

The original compares functional and structural networks across Lewy body dementia hallucination groups. Clinical ratings distinguish degrees of frequency and severity. Imaging and clinical associations do not test eating dried figs.

The systematic review covers cannabinoid treatments in neurocognitive disorders with behavioral, motor and safety outcomes. The exposures are cannabinoids in the reviewed forms. No source evaluates dried fig or a fig-linked Parkinson visual outcome.

The radiotracer review examines methods for imaging α-synuclein-related disorders. Visual phenomenology is clinical context. The tracer studies leave the culinary exposure and episode-rate outcome unexamined.

The population-based PINE cohort follows incident Parkinson disease and comparison participants for dementia. Clinical symptom histories are potential predictors. The rate measured is dementia incidence, with no fig-related change in visual episodes.

The Movement Disorder Society criteria specify diagnostic levels and features for multiple system atrophy. Early hallucinations enter differential diagnosis. There is no Parkinson culinary symptom comparison.

The ParkWest cohort uses predefined clinical thresholds for onset of hallucinations and other disease milestones, then analyzes mortality. Reaching a clinical threshold is distinct from changes in repeated visual episodes. The cohort does not compare dried fig intake.

The review synthesizes resting-state connectivity studies in neurodegenerative conditions with hallucinations. Eleven eligible articles contribute imaging comparisons with heterogeneous symptoms. It does not identify a fig exposure or causal dietary outcome.

The multiplex family study reports clinicopathological patterns of multiple system atrophy and Parkinson disease with dementia. Visual experiences are reported in a family history. The pedigree does not supply an exposure comparison or food-related change.

This 56-person exploratory study compares visual experience descriptions in schizophrenia, post-traumatic stress disorder and the combination. The measures concern psychiatric groups and trauma-related contexts. No Parkinson fig intake or comparable clinical episode rate is measured.

The paper combines a Parkinson case associated with an LRRK2 variant and patient-derived cellular comparisons. The original exposure contrast concerns genotype and laboratory function. It does not test dried fig or clinical visual episodes.

The disease review describes GBA-related Parkinson phenotypes and laboratory findings, citing reports of visual hallucinations. The cited genotype and clinical associations do not measure a dried fig response.

Outpatient examinations in 25 nonadvanced Parkinson cases compare selected ocular and visual functions. Hallucinations are discussed as one of several possible disturbances. No exposure-linked visual episode outcome is supplied.

The study compares item patterns on a cognitive screening examination for different dementia diagnoses. Hallucinations are considered as adjunct diagnostic information. The cognitive scoring analysis does not track fig intake or episode frequency.

The review compares clinical criteria for multiple system atrophy with overlapping diagnoses. Hallucinations are discussed as a discriminator with timing and medication caveats. The source provides no culinary comparison.

In a small postmortem Parkinson series, six of eight patients had a visual hallucination history. The inspected tissue measures did not show a clear correlation with hallucination presence in the reported regions. The finding is about pathology and a binary history, without dietary exposure.

The MRI cohort compares 16 Parkinson visual hallucinators, 75 Parkinson nonhallucinators and 32 controls. Dynamic network states are the outcomes. Classification by clinical report does not establish a dietary cause or measured change in visual episodes.

The clinical comparison covers 92 dementia with Lewy bodies cases and 93 Parkinson dementia cases. It examines geriatric syndromes and their co-occurrence. Nutrition-related and visual features are separate clinical observations without a measured fig exposure.

The systematic review and meta-analysis evaluate structural network measures in Parkinson disease. Clinical diversity, including nonmotor features, is noted as a limitation. The pooled imaging measures do not estimate food or visual symptom effects.

The multicenter clinical study compares symptom and cognitive profiles by sex in Lewy body disease. Visual hallucinations are a clinical variable. The study is not an oral exposure comparison or a measure of episodes after eating dried fig.

The article describes longitudinal phenotyping and specimen collection for multiple system atrophy cohorts. It includes a planned or administered hallucination inventory as one clinical instrument. There is no dried fig exposure or Parkinson meal-linked result.

The laboratory study compares a defined anionic membrane lipid with recombinant protein variants in biochemical assays. The lipid is a model membrane material. The outcomes are in vitro measurements without a clinical, edible fig or hallucination comparison.

The Global Multiple System Atrophy Registry survey records patient-reported symptoms, including a proportion who answered that they saw things that were absent. It examines association with levodopa history and discusses diagnostic uncertainty. It does not track fig consumption or episode counts.

The dry eye review pools prevalence and ocular signs in Parkinson disease. Visual hallucinations appear among broader ocular complaints. The measured question concerns dryness, with no dried fig or repeated hallucination comparison.

The MRI comparison evaluates optic radiation features in Lewy body disease grouped by visual hallucination status. Imaging and a clinical history indicator are the relevant measurements. It does not compare dietary exposures.

The radiological review surveys GABAergic system imaging in Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism. It references visual hallucinations and separate postmortem evidence. No dried fig or clinical visual episode intervention is studied.

The preclinical article studies disease-related protein and neurological model outcomes. Human hallucinations appear in the clinical framing of some inherited cases. The experimental outcomes provide no evidence on eating dried figs or patient visual episodes.

The review discusses clinical translation of cell therapies in Parkinson disease. It distinguishes motor restoration from persistent nonmotor symptoms reported after referenced interventions. These are nonfood therapies and their outcomes do not address dried fig.

The clinical record analysis compares treatment and outcome risks among Parkinson patients with and without psychosis and across medication choices. Hallucinations contribute to the clinical syndrome. Neither the treatment groups nor the measurements identify a fig exposure.

The review compares Parkinson retinal imaging and functional retinal measurements. Visual hallucinations appear among several perceptual features and in referenced comparisons. The article supplies no evidence on dried fig intake or episode changes.

The 20-item noise task tests whether perceiving nonexistent targets in ambiguous images distinguishes Parkinson participants with a complex hallucination history. Its sensitivity and specificity depend on the task-error threshold. This is a diagnostic task response rather than a dietary effect.

The molecular review discusses early synaptic changes and α-synuclein in neurodegeneration. Visual hallucinations characterize clinical groups in the discussion. It has no human fig exposure or visual episode-frequency outcome.

The review summarizes diagnostic performance of functional dopaminergic scintigraphy in Lewy body dementia. Hallucination history appears in diagnostic criteria and cited study context. It does not measure food intake or changes in visual symptoms.

The retrospective MRI study compares brainstem structure in dementia with Lewy bodies, progressive supranuclear palsy and Parkinson disease. Visual hallucinations are part of the diagnostic background. Brainstem morphometry is not an exposure-linked episode measure.

The review systematically compares structural, task-based and resting-state neuroimaging in Parkinson complex and minor hallucinations. Differences in symptom definition and scales are noted. None of the reviewed contrasts measures a specified fig exposure.

The longitudinal clinic cohort describes early-onset Parkinson progression. Visual hallucinations occurred in some cases and were discussed against later-onset presentations. The study supplies no preparation-specific dietary exposure or timing of episodes after eating.

The ONDRI analysis relates cerebrovascular imaging and cortical measures to neuropsychiatric scales across diagnostic cohorts. Its references distinguish visual hallucinations from other questionnaire domains. The anatomical and symptom-scale associations do not test fig ingestion.

The review considers lipids and proteins in synucleinopathy pathology. Visual hallucinations motivate discussion of affected regions. The review describes lipid homeostasis rather than culinary fig exposure or episode changes in patients.

The FDG-PET study compares analytical methods and glucose-metabolism maps across Lewy body spectrum groups. Visual hallucinations are clinical context. Tracer uptake does not measure fig or dietary glucose intake.

A cross-sectional Parkinson comparison tests reasoning with a beads task and assesses psychosis and impulsivity. The reported task performance did not clearly associate with Parkinson psychosis. It does not test an exposure-linked change in visual hallucinations.

The noise pareidolia task results are interpreted in relation to visuoperceptual performance and reported hallucinations. The findings do not justify treating a laboratory false perception as an equivalent measure of a spontaneous episode. There is no fig exposure.

The narrative review focuses on apathy prevalence, mechanisms and treatments across dementias. Visual hallucinations appear as a separate co-occurring feature in cited studies. It provides no dried fig or visual symptom intervention.

The hypothesis review proposes thalamic mechanisms spanning neurodegeneration, psychiatric psychosis and experimentally altered perception. Observations come from those separate populations and exposures. It does not supply a fig-specific human effect.

Transcriptome-based modeling predicts candidate metabolic changes and cites an earlier urinary salsolinol comparison in levodopa-treated patients. Neither the modeled estimates nor the cited figure establishes fig content or any food-linked clinical visual effect.

The retrospective Parkinson study compares motor progression across the timing of REM sleep behavior disorder. Clinical sleep and associated nonmotor history characterize the groups. The outcome does not measure food or visual episodes after eating.

The multicenter clinical-pathological analysis relates substantia nigra cell loss and clinical features by sex. Hallucinations are self- or caregiver-reported clinical features. Tissue loss and symptom history cannot identify a fig-related episode effect.

The rodent study compares neurophysiological measures under experimental treatments in a Parkinson psychosis model. Human visual hallucinations motivate the model. The recorded animal signals are not observed clinical visual episodes or evidence of dried fig effects.

The virtual reality and patient analyses report estimation bias and induced sensed presence. Clinical groups and exclusions distinguish sensed presence from formed visual hallucinations. The test does not identify an oral food exposure or assess episode rate after ingestion.

The study relates white matter neurite measures to amyloid and tau in people on the Lewy body dementia spectrum. Formed hallucination history is part of clinical group characterization. The imaging outcome leaves a dietary episode contrast unanswered.

The 154-person Parkinson cohort examines sex differences and associations between sleep and nonmotor domains. The perception and hallucination domain is a symptom-scale measurement. Neither diet nor dried fig was assigned or compared.

The review evaluates vitamin B12 and other nutrient findings, including Parkinson risk, peripheral neuropathy and treatment-related context. Nutrient associations and food intake references provide no measured fig exposure combined with a visual episode outcome.

The pragmatic review distinguishes prodromal Lewy body dementia from prodromal Alzheimer presentations. It emphasizes clinical features including early visual hallucinations and fluctuations. These are diagnostic observations without a fig efficacy comparison.

The frontotemporal dementia study compares attentional, memory and imaging profiles by reported hallucination status and relevant genotype. It distinguishes a visual subgroup. Its disorder, measurements and exposure differ from the frozen Parkinson food premise.

The MRI comparison includes 28 people with Lewy body disease and visual experiences, separating minor and complex phenomena in ratings. It associates regional structure with symptom characteristics. It contains no food exposure or time-linked change after dried fig.

The longitudinal PPMI analysis considers blood cell ratio and cognitive-performance trajectories. Visual hallucinations appear in background on cognitive-risk features. The blood marker and cognitive endpoint do not evaluate dried fig.

The retrospective case series describes progressive supranuclear palsy phenotypes in people of South Asian descent. Visual hallucinations prompted consideration of alternative diagnoses in some cases. It supplies no reported fig exposure or diet-linked Parkinson episode rate.

Records of 2,204 people diagnosed with very late-onset psychosis are followed for dementia outcomes. Visual hallucinations and other Lewy body features at onset are predictors. The follow-up outcome is dementia, without a dietary exposure or Parkinson episode-rate contrast.

The clinical review assesses diagnostic evidence using α-synuclein assays across disorders. Hallucinations characterize the Lewy body spectrum. The comparison addresses diagnostic biomarkers without a fig exposure or episode outcome.

The study of drug-naïve Parkinson participants compares MRI associations with pareidolia task performance and separately reported visual hallucinations. Distinct imaging patterns are reported. The study contains no dried fig intake or changes in spontaneous episodes after eating.
